articles.content:
Spain , the Country of Honor at this year's International Film Festival of India (IFFI), made its case to Indian filmmakers at WAVES Film Bazaar in Goa, laying out its incentives, locations and crews and pushing for closer co-production ties.

The panel, "Spain: Where Stories Find Their Stage – Incentives, Locations & Co-production Opportunities," was part of the Knowledge Series at the 20th edition of the market, which runs Nov. 20-24 alongside the 57th IFFI. "For us, co-production is a key instrument," said Camilo Vázquez, deputy director of the Institute of Cinematography and Audiovisual Arts (ICAA), the film agency of Spain's Ministry of Culture. He pointed to better financing, exchanges between technical and artistic teams, and stories that could connect with audiences in both countries, and described the timing as particularly favorable for India-Spain partnerships.

For Indian producers weighing Spain as a filming destination, the offer extends beyond its locations. Usha Jadhav, a National Award-winning actor and producer with Spanish company ACortes Films, highlighted the country's track record with international productions, its range of landscapes and architecture, and skilled crews used to working on both big-budget and independent films. She also cited eight-hour shifts and quieter shooting environments as practical advantages, particularly for sync-sound productions.

Jadhav said the relationship should not be limited to service work, and made a case for collaborations that bring creative teams together across borders. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Language is not a barrier, because cinema itself is a universal language," Jadhav said. "We need human stories."

Lara Molina, general coordinator of the Spain Film Commission, outlined the tax incentives available to international productions. Miguel Fabián Salazar, Spain's economic and commercial counselor in Mumbai for the country's trade and investment agency ICEX, set out what each side brings. India offers production scale, a large consumer market, a global diaspora and strengths in VFX and animation. Spain offers experienced crews, creative talent and access to Europe and Latin America. Partnerships could run from co-production and financing to distribution, post-production and production services.

"These points somehow fit together. They are not exclusive. They all feed into each other," Salazar said, noting that Spanish films and productions were traveling farther internationally while Indian productions and streaming services were growing fast.

ICEX's Mumbai office works with producers and distributors on market access, local partnerships, setting up businesses and regulatory requirements. It has also organized business missions involving Indian companies in animation, post-production and gaming.

For Indian producers looking to develop a project with Spanish partners, Guillermo Rodríguez, director of the Valladolid-based cultural institution Casa de la India, said: "The real roadmap is about building connections and building trust."

India and Spain signed their audiovisual co-production agreement in 2012. Rodríguez said the scheme was being updated and that clear guidelines would be issued.

"If you plan to shoot in both countries or one of the countries, you have to make sure you follow those guidelines precisely. Under the co-production agreement, an Indian producer has to approach NFDC… and the Spanish co-producer has to go to ICAA," he said.

NFDC is India's National Film Development Corporation.

The session closed with a showcase of five Spanish projects seeking Indian collaborators. These included "My Parents Grand Bazaar," the feature debut of Andalusian filmmaker Rakesh Narwani; "Serendipia," an India-Mexico-Spain romance; "The Dragon Letter," from Ladakh-born director Stanzin Jigmet, based on his short of the same name, which won gold in the narrative category at the 2026 Student Academy Awards; animated project "Mumu"; and documentary "Aana and Aai – The War to Become an Artist." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Rodríguez noted that the two countries had largely stuck to familiar markets, with Spain looking toward Europe and Latin America and India toward English-speaking territories.

"Imagine the global Indian industry working with the Spanish-speaking world," he said. "Because Spain is not just Spain. It's access to the entire Spanish-speaking world – over 500 million people. So if you can bring those two cultural superpowers together, imagine the potential."

articles.title: Clayface Streaming Release Date Revealed as the $30 Million Film Passes the DCU’s Biggest Bomb at the Box Office
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Warner Bros. Only 45 days after its theatrical release, Clayface is coming to digital with an announced release date of December 8. This is a pretty big deal, as the movie is still thriving at the box office, making more money, which has ensured it is profitable thanks to the lower budget that James Gunn set so […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Only 45 days after its theatrical release, Clayface is coming to digital with an announced release date of December 8. This is a pretty big deal, as the movie is still thriving at the box office, making more money, which has ensured it is profitable thanks to the lower budget that James Gunn set so it could be a success as an offbeat comic book horror movie. Clayface tells the story of an actor named Matt Hagen, who was disfigured by the local mafia. When he agreed to an experimental procedure, he became the supervillain Clayface and sought revenge.

Clayface hits digital on December 8, which is a pretty normal wait for a horror movie like this. While movies like Superman had a longer run in theaters as big-budget spectacle releases, films like Clayface become available a lot quicker because of the niche genre. This announcement also came the same weekend that Clayface passed the $126 million mark at the box office, coming close to surpassing Supergirl's total .

CLAYFACE takes shape on Digital December 8th. Over 45 days after its theatrical debut 🫠 pic.twitter.com/kvTnVKMBbv

On the same weekend that the Clayface digital release was announced, Clayface was still rolling along in its theatrical run . It passed the $126 million mark at the worldwide box office. Superman made $618.7 million on a $225 million budget. Supergirl only made $126.5 million on a $170 million budget, taking a huge loss at the box office. Knowing a horror movie would make less money, James Gunn produced Clayface on a low $40 million budget, which makes its current box office take of $126.2 million a clear profit. The film will pass Supergirl this week.

That is a big deal because it proved that James Gunn knew what he was doing when setting up Clayface for its release, ensuring it was able to make a profit thanks to the lower budget. This didn't make up for the loss that Supergirl experienced, but that was a special case where it started off at a disadvantage. It is also important to note that this will probably be the last time DC releases a movie anything like Clayface , since the new people in charge are not likely to take chances on properties like this and will focus solely on the big-name characters from now on.

For fans who loved what Clayface offered, though, it will arrive in just a few short weeks on digital and allow people to have the movie at home to enjoy. It shouldn't take long after that for it to arrive on HBO Max, and the Blu-ray and 4K release will probably come in January, since it takes an average of anywhere from two weeks to eight weeks to receive a physical release after the digital.

articles.title: A $1.8 Billion Action Fantasy Epic Has Sailed to Streaming Success and It Would be a Tragedy Not to Watch It
articles.summary: Courtesy of Universal Pictures There have been many epic stories told based on Greek myths and legends. Many of them have become huge box office successes thanks to the fascination with tales of monsters and heroes from a time long forgotten, and that includes one of the biggest movies of the decade. Released earlier this year in competition with […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There have been many epic stories told based on Greek myths and legends. Many of them have become huge box office successes thanks to the fascination with tales of monsters and heroes from a time long forgotten, and that includes one of the biggest movies of the decade. Released earlier this year in competition with summer blockbusters like Spider-Man: Brand New Day , Christopher Nolan followed up his Oscar-winning Oppenheimer with probably his most unexpected project today a mega-budget retelling of The Odyssey . After making a huge profit in cinemas - despite an equally massive budget - Nolan's biggest film to date has now arrived on PVOD and instantly dominated several streaming platforms hosting the movie including Apple Store and Amazon. Despite millions turning out to see the star-studded spectacle in theaters, it seems that just as many are now watching it at home and you probably should watch it too if you haven't seen it yet.

The Odyssey is a story that has been told many times over the last century, in TV shows and on the big screen. However, there have been few versions like Christopher Nolan's retelling, which does for Greek myth what he did for Batman and bring a gritty grounded feel to a story full of wonder and fantasy. The story of Odysseus making his dangerous journey home after the Trojan War includes plenty of action, fearsome monsters, and converging storylines that bring The Odyssey to life like never before with some of the biggest actors in Hollywood right now filling a stacked cast. Matt Damon plays Odysseus, and he is ably helped by Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Jon Bernthal, Zendaya, Charlize Theron, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong'o and more. Of course, it would not be a Christopher Nolan movie without backing up this talented cast with some kind groundbreaking filmmaking process and Nolan did not disappoint in this either.

Christopher Nolan's love of movies is well-documented, so it came as no surprise that the director wanted to make The Odyssey with the final cinematic experience in mind. This resulted in him capturing his movie entirely on IMAX film cameras, a first for any film and a task that used over two million feet of 70mm film to make Nolan's vision a reality. While many of those watching in regular cinemas were not able to appreciate this extra effort, The Odyssey took over the vast majority of IMAX screens around the world on its release, meaning there were a lot of cinefiles and Nolan fans able to experience the film with the breathtaking scale he intended. The takeover of IMAX cinemas, with its higher ticket prices, did not hurt when it came to pushing the movie's box office total to $1.8 billion worldwide.

Nolan's record-breaking run did not stop with the making of the movie. The movie gave Nolan his highest ever opening weekend gross, surpassing the $248 million of The Dark Knight Rises with a total of $264.1, as well as being the highest grossing R-rated movie, Universal Pictures' movie, and Nolan-directed film. For a movie seen by many as a huge gamble, and one that generated plenty of forthright opinions on social media for several casting decisions, it paid off massively for everyone involved. Additionally, it continued Nolan's streak of highly praised films, earning a 94% RT score, making it Nolan's best reviewed movie. Now that the film is available at home on PVOD services, many who decided to skip The Odyssey in cinemas are discovering the towering achievement by Nolan that begs the question of what he can possible do to top it. Will he follow it up with The Iliad as fellow director Steven Spielberg has suggested? We can only wait and see, but after The Odyssey 's massive success Universal would probably have no issues greenlighting the movie if Nolan chose to do it.

Would you like to see Nolan return to Greek myth again for his next movie? Have you seen The Odyssey yet? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: Is the New Doomsday Trailer Coming Monday? MCU Star’s Post Makes It Even More Likely
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel It seems that one Avengers: Doomsday star has hinted at when people might expect to see the final trailer for the upcoming Marvel Cinematic Universe movie. There has been a lot of talk about the next trailer for the movie, and there are even hints that it will be an incredibly emotional trailer, which suggests […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google It seems that one Avengers: Doomsday star has hinted at when people might expect to see the final trailer for the upcoming Marvel Cinematic Universe movie. There has been a lot of talk about the next trailer for the movie, and there are even hints that it will be an incredibly emotional trailer, which suggests it will show a lot more than the past trailers. So far, there have been teasers that hinted at who was going to be in the movie, a bigger trailer that showed the heroes planning to fight Doctor Doom, and the most recent one focused on Doom with more of a look at Captain America.

It seems like Simu Liu has teased the upcoming arrival of the next Avengers: Doomsday trailer. This came from two posts on his Instagram Stories. The first had an emoji of a clock set to 10:10, and the second had a winking face. This has led people to believe that the new Avengers: Doomsday trailer will finally arrive on Monday, and this is something that most MCU fans have been waiting for.

Simu Liu is seemingly teasing the final trailer for ‘AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY’ via Instagram: “🕰️😉” pic.twitter.com/aiUEvpTPtT

The new Avengers: Doomsday trailer, expected to hit on Monday, was previously teased by Hayley Atwell , who plays Peggy Carter in the MCU. With Simu Liu now hinting at its arrival, it seems that what Atwell teased might be coming as early as tomorrow morning. This will likely give a lot more footage of Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, but the idea that it might be an emotional trailer makes it seem like there will be a lot more shown concerning possible deaths or even the end of certain worlds.

Remember, Avengers: Doomsday is based on the Marvel Comics storyline "Time Runs Out," which saw the incursions destroying every Earth in the multiverse, an event that counts down to only two Earths remaining. From the look of it, those two Earths might be Earth-616 with the Avengers and the X-Men's Earth, which is where the original Fox X-Men cast is returning, along with some fun additions like Channing Tatum's Gambit showing back up again after his appearance in Deadpool & Wolverine . There are also rumors of other Earths, including Tobey Maguire's Spider-Man Earth. Could the emotional footage be showing something like Maguire's Earth being destroyed?

There is also the chance that the emotions could come from the death of someone important being shown in the trailer, and the idea that it could be Patrick Stewart's Professor X could be something that could devastate audiences. Honestly, it will probably not show any of that, with Marvel saving the surprises, deaths, and destruction for the movie itself. Instead, it might play into the feelings people have for the old X-Men and Spider-Man movies , and how this could finally end those stories for good. Whatever it is, Simu Liu makes it seem like Monday will be when the trailer drops.

articles.title: Marvel Heroes Are Having an Identity Crisis, and It's About More Than Secret Identities
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Comics If you've been reading modern Marvel, there's one storyline that's been recurring multiple times across numerous comics. Superheroes keep having their identities stolen in one capacity or another. This has become especially prevalent with some of the heroes' most iconic villains, with prominent examples being Norman Osborn temporarily taking over as Spider-Man without Peter's permission […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google If you've been reading modern Marvel , there's one storyline that's been recurring multiple times across numerous comics. Superheroes keep having their identities stolen in one capacity or another. This has become especially prevalent with some of the heroes' most iconic villains, with prominent examples being Norman Osborn temporarily taking over as Spider-Man without Peter's permission and the Eldest stealing the Hulk's body in the pages of Infernal Hulk . On the surface, this doesn't appear to be anything out of the ordinary, as heroes are plenty known to share similar stories across the board, but this goes far deeper than simple circular and mirrored storytelling.

This is actually a reflection of a major change in how Marvel treats its superheroes. When they were first created, the vast majority of them were meant to embody the world-outside-your-window perspective, being portrayed as more down-to-earth and less paragon-esque than DC's heroes were in the Silver and Bronze Ages. That's continued to this day, to some extent, but that barrier has been breaking down steadily over decades. Nowadays, Marvel's heroes are ideals given human form, and the reason villains keep taking their faces is to explicitly relate to how important the heroes have become to us.

Back in the 1960s, Marvel sought to differentiate itself from DC by offering a different type of hero. The vast majority of DC's catalogue at the time was taken up by paragons who could do no wrong, from Superman to Wonder Woman to Batman. Their stories were often simplistic, and thus their ideologies were often portrayed the same way. Marvel challenged that by grounding its heroes in the then-modern day with deeply personal struggles. Think of the family drama inherent to the Fantastic Four or Spider-Man's efforts to balance making rent with his superheroic duties. This resulted in heroes who felt rougher around the edges, in a way. They made more unjustifiable mistakes than DC's heroes did.

However, it didn't stay that way forever. Over time, Marvel started portraying its heroes in a more traditional DC way, while DC's own heroes took on deeper, more human flaws. Spider-Man is a perfect example . In his earliest years, Peter was a brash, abrasive young man who had a chip on his shoulder the size of Texas. Yet, as he did more and more heroics, that part naturally faded away. Modern portrayals of Peter, even when they tackle the start of his career, portray him as the wiser, more centered hero that he's become. You could accuse this of Marvel sanitizing Peter in some way, and that may be a part of it, but the reason that this happens across the board is that these heroes have come to mean something much more to fans over the years.

The moments that stick with the most fans the most are when heroes are at their most heroic. Spider-Man pushing past his limits to save Aunt May. Hulk choosing to forgive the Leader and himself. These moments are noble and heroic in their truest sense, so as the hero continues to develop, these moments and interpretations stick when other aspects don't. Repeated moments like this have elevated the heroes from characters who tried to be heroic to the very faces of what it means to embody those ideals. They've become more and more like paragons, more and more like modern myths meant to inspire. Which brings us to why so many villains want to take those heroes' identities.

The supervillain stealing a hero's identity storyline has become a true epidemic. In the past few years alone, it's happened to most of Marvel's biggest names. The Edlest has taken the Hulk's body, Norman impersonated Spider-Man, Grant Rogers is back to pretending to be Captain America, and more. This idea of someone else becoming a hero has expanded to an entire subgenre, including different takes on it like A.I.M. attempting to make their own Tony Stark, not Iron Man, and Beta Ray Bill grappling with the reality of everyone thinking he was Thor after the God of Thunder was erased from existence. It's going on across the board, and the answer isn't as simple as villains wanting to abuse everyone's faith in these heroes. Rather, it's an examination of what these heroes stand for.

This happens to Cap , Spider-Man, and Hulk more than anyone else, and there's a reason for that. The first two are the de facto paragons of Marvel, representing the peak of the heroism all others strive to emulate. The Hulk, meanwhile, has always served as a window into the inner rage and anguish that a person could go through, and how working through that or living with it could work. These three are ideas just as much as they are characters, which makes them perfect to contrast against others who steal or borrow their names.

Whenever someone steals one of these superheroic identities, the story itself serves as an argument of what it is that makes that person a hero. We look through all of their choices and actions, and come to the conclusion that these characters have risen to the ranks that they have because they always attempt to do the right thing. By juxtaposing the hero's success to how these villains fail to live up to those standards or miss the point, it highlights how special the heroes are. They have fully transitioned from being characters to being something greater, and there's no better way to show that than by direct comparison.

Marvel's writers have been exploring the place heroes have in the world not as individuals, but as ideas to strive for. Spider-Man is someone who struggles but always puts being responsible over personal gain. Captain America is a man who will never stop fighting for liberty and equality. These characters mean something more to people, and thus they are being treated more as myths and explorations of what people wish to be over standard protagonists. Simply put, Marvel's heroes have been constantly getting more heroic, and the best way to dissect that is with villains who show us everything that the heroes aren't.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Invincible is coming back for a fifth season, and while the comics paint a pretty good picture of what will happen in the coming episodes, several things are still up in the air. After all, the Prime Video series has already made a ton of changes to the Image Comics run, with season 4 even introducing an original storyline centered around Damien Darkblood.

With a teaser for Invincible season 5 now released , the show's return is finally starting to feel close. So, ahead of season 5's premiere on February 17, 2027, here are five characters from the Invincible comics that I can't wait to see make their debut in the animated series. WARNING: Contains spoilers for the Invincible comics .

One of the only characters we know will debut in Invincible season 5 is Gravitator. Gravitator is a street-level villain whose real name is Chris, a factory worker who began his criminal career so that he could buy an engagement ring. So, he builds an anti-gravity suit and robs a bank, although he is caught in the act by Invincible. After a couple of missteps and another encounter with Invincible, Mark realizes that Chris has the potential to be a good person. So, he puts him in contact with the GDA, where Chris goes on to work.

Jack Quaid has been cast as Gravitator in Invincible season 5 , and it'll be incredibly exciting to see the actor take on another superhero role. Quaid rose to popularity due to his role as Hughie in Prime Video's adaptation of The Boys . However, he has also proven himself to be a talented superhero voice actor thanks to his title role in My Adventures with Superman .

If Markus Murphy does appear in Invincible , it probably won't be in season 5. After all, the character makes his debut in issue #129, while season 4 wrapped up with the reveal that the Viltrumites have assimilated to Earth in the wake of the Viltrumite War, which occurs in issue #77. So, season 6 seems like a more likely time for Markus to make his debut. However, it is possible that a scene directly linked to Markus' first appearance may occur in season 5, if it happens at all.

In the comics, Markus is the son of Mark Grayson. He was conceived after Anissa, the Viltrumite villain who has already appeared several times throughout the series, sexually assaulted Mark in an attempt to continue the Viltrumite bloodline. This is one of the most controversial scenes from the comics, and since the Prime Video series has avoided some of the source material's controversial subjects, it'll be interesting to see how Invincible handles the Anissa and Markus storyline.

In Invincible season 4, Robot and Monster Girl enter the Flaxan Dimension in order to save Earth by closing the Flaxan portal. However, they become stuck on the other side, with them ending the season trapped in a universe where time occurs much faster. Season 5 will undoubtedly continue this storyline , which is one of the most interesting ones from the Invincible comics. Thus, it wouldn't be surprising for season 5 to feature the debut of Monster Girl's son, Monax Zaxal.

After spending decades in the Flaxan Dimension, Robot manages to overthrow the alien government and rebuild Flaxan society. Throughout the years, Robot's increasingly authoritarian actions cause Monster Girl to resent him, with her eventually leading a rebellion against his rule. While they are apart, Monster Girl and another Flaxan have a child named Monax. Eventually, Monax makes his way to Earth, with him seeking revenge on Robot.

Terra Grayson is arguably the most significant Invincible comics character who hasn't appeared in the show yet, and I can't wait for her to make her debut. As the daughter of Mark and Atom Eve, Terra is gifted with all the powers of a Viltrumite, immediately making her one of the most powerful characters in the Invincible universe. Terra makes her debut in issue #113, and while she probably won't be present in season 5, it is likely that the upcoming episodes will set the stage for Terra to appear in the following season.

Terra is key to many of the later Invincible stories, and she will become increasingly important as the series nears its end. Since so much of Invincible so far has been about the relationship between Nolan and Mark, it'll be interesting to see how the show handles putting Mark in the parental role with Terra. There are tons of interesting themes that could be explored with this storyline, and it'll add another layer to the world of Invincible .

It is a near-guarantee that we will see all of the aforementioned Invincible characters before the Prime Video series ends. Spawn, on the other hand, has already missed his opportunity to show up. Created by Todd McFarlane, Spawn is the most iconic Image Comics superhero, with him having a 1990s HBO animated series and a 1997 live-action feature film. After dying, going to Hell, and making a deal with a demon, the hero is brought back to Earth as a Hellspawn, where he attempts to atone for his past sins by fighting evil.

Spawn appears in the Invincible comics as an Image Comics crossover character, with him showing up during major events like the Invincible War. Initially, no characters who originated outside of Invincible appeared in the Prime Video show, with them being replaced by other Invincible heroes and villains. However, seasons 3 and 4 have featured previously missing crossover characters, like Tech Jacket, Brit, and the Astounding Wolf-Man. Unfortunately, Spawn has still been left out of the series . While television rights are probably behind Spawn's exclusion, I hope Prime Video manages to pull off a cameo before Invincible ends.

articles.title: 6 Great Crime Films to Watch When You Eventually Need A Break From GTA VI
articles.summary: It is impossible not to have heard about the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, as gamers across the globe are now playing one of the most highly anticipated video games of all time. Rockstar's newest release has received critical acclaim and is currently claiming hours of attention from anyone who has purchased it. No […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google It is impossible not to have heard about the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , as gamers across the globe are now playing one of the most highly anticipated video games of all time. Rockstar's newest release has received critical acclaim and is currently claiming hours of attention from anyone who has purchased it.

No matter how incredible the game is, a binge session can only go so long. Eventually, fans are going to want a break. Luckily, these six crime films will scratch the same itch as GTA VI , keeping viewers in the zone before they drop back into Vice City.

Michael Mann's 2004 film Collateral is one of the greatest movies of the 2000s, and it still holds up nearly two decades (and several GTA games) later. The film follows Jamie Foxx's Max Durocher, a Los Angeles cab driver who is given an incredibly high fare to drive to several locations with Tom Cruise's Vincent. Eventually, Max discovers that Vincent is a hitman, making the driver an accomplice to his crimes. So, Max must play his cards right in order to survive the night, escape Vincent, and avoid any trouble from the fallout of the killings.

Collateral has all of the key elements that make a GTA game, such as automotive crime, violent killings , and a seedy criminal underworld. The film takes place in LA, which is parodied in the GTA V setting, Los Santos. Plus, GTA VI actually references Collateral , as players can have an encounter where an NPC inspired by Vincent takes Jason hostage and forces him to drive a taxi around. So, before getting to this moment in the game, it's a good idea to check out Collateral .

This isn't the first or the last time that a Michael Mann film will appear on this list, but 1995's Heat is arguably the director's best film , and it fits perfectly into the vibe of GTA VI . Set in Los Angeles, the film follows the cat-and-mouse game between Al Pacino's LAPD detective Vincent Hanna and Robert De Niro's aging career criminal Neil McCauley. The near-three-hour epic kicks off with an iconic sequence in which an armored car is robbed, and the ball doesn't stop rolling until the credits.

Heat features intricately planned, large-scale robberies and a cast of criminal characters, and it's not hard to see how the film inspired the GTA franchise. On top of that, the film hinges on a tense chase of a cop trying to catch a criminal. Much of the fun of the GTA games is trying to help your criminal player character evade the police, and while Heat is a bit more dramatic, it perfectly captures this conflict.

Directed by Ridley Scott, the mastermind behind Alien and Blade Runner , 1991's Thelma & Louise is one of the director's most underrated films. The film stars Geena Davis as Thelma and Susan Sarandon as Louise, two friends who decide to go on a weekend fishing trip. While on the way, the duo kills an attempted rapist at a bar. So, they decide to flee to Mexico, with them driving their 1996 Ford Thunderbird convertible across the country as the FBI pursues them. The film was critically acclaimed, with it being nominated for six Oscars and winning Best Original Screenplay. Tragically, the film hasn't received the same mainstream notoriety as some of Scott's franchise films.

Like some of the other films on this list, Thelma & Louise is about characters running away from the police. However, the chase is far more literal in this film, as the police are always just one step behind the duo. Like in GTA , the main characters have to evade police cars and helicopters, and they occasionally have to survive encounters with the authorities while keeping their identities hidden.

Released only a year before Jaws , 1974's The Sugarland Express is one of legendary director Steven Spielberg's lesser-known films. However, it is just as good as any of the filmmaker's other masterpieces. The film stars Goldie Hawn as Lou Jean and William Atherton as Clovis, the latter of whom begins the film incarcerated. Lou Jean pays Clovis a visit to inform him that their son will soon be placed in foster care. So, they steal a car, take a police officer hostage, and go on the run from the authorities as they attempt to reach their son.

Players of GTA VI should immediately be able to see the parallels. Like The Sugarland Express , GTA VI follows a criminal couple who, after one of them gets out of prison, attempt to regain custody of their young child. Both the film and the game feature a massive amount of police vehicles getting involved in chases, and a world of crime centered around a surprisingly tender relationship.

When it comes to movies centered around a police chase, it is impossible to think of one more iconic than Hal Needham's 1977 film Smokey and the Bandit . The film follows two criminals, Burt Reynolds' Bo "Bandit" Darville and Jerry Reed's Cledus "The Snowman" Snow, who are tasked with illegally transporting a large supply of Coors beer from Texarkana to Atlanta for some wealthy benefactors. Knowing that law enforcement will be on their tail, they devise a plan. Snowman will drive the truck full of beer, while the Bandit will act as a blocker, using his iconic 1977 Pontiac Trans Am to distract police. However, they never could have expected how persistent Jackie Gleason's Sheriff Buford T. Justice would be.

Smokey and the Bandit is a film about transporting an illegal drug while evading law enforcement by way of reckless driving. It is hard to think of a film that could be more GTA than that. Plus, the film's Southern setting makes it not too far off from GTA VI 's South Florida setting, with the film's cast resembling some of the side characters in the game.

Michael Mann is a master of the crime genre, and no film from throughout cinematic history could be a better companion piece to GTA VI than the director's 2006 take on Miami Vice . Based on the iconic 1980s TV show, Miami Vice stars Colin Farrell as Sonny and Jamie Foxx as Rico, two officers from the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office who work together to take on the world of illegal narcotics.

Miami Vice is all over the DNA of GTA VI , with the game's setting even paying tribute to the franchise by being named Vice City. The game's blue and pink color scheme is directly ripped from the original show, and while this isn't as present in the 2006 film, it occasionally pops up. A game based on GTA VI would feel exactly like Miami Vice , and until one gets made, this is the closest to a GTA movie adaptation that we have.

What crime movies remind you of GTA ? Let us know on the ComicBook Forum !

articles.title: Doctor Who's First Major Action Figure Line Was Infamously Bad, But Fans Couldn't Get Enough of It
articles.summary: Action figure collectors today sometimes forget how good we have it. Today’s world of collector-focused toylines means any property, no matter how obscure, is fair game for an action figure line. But going back a few decades, this was hardly the case: conventional wisdom held that the primary target for any toys were children, and […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Action figure collectors today sometimes forget how good we have it. Today’s world of collector-focused toylines means any property, no matter how obscure, is fair game for an action figure line. But going back a few decades, this was hardly the case: conventional wisdom held that the primary target for any toys were children, and as such, any toyline had to be something manufacturers could see kids wanting. Doctor Who , despite being a decades-running staple of British television, somehow avoided almost any toy merchandising during its original, twenty-six year lifetime. Denys-Fisher (Mego’s U.K. affiliate) released a small range of Doctor Who figures in 1977 and 1978; several companies offered Daleks; but for many collectors, the dream was an extensive, Star Wars -style line of characters from across eras and Doctors. 

Model train manufacturer Dapol finally delivered in 1987, although with perhaps underwhelming results. That didn’t stop Doctor Who fans from turning out in force to collect the line – at least at first. The Dapol Doctor Who line was plagued with problems, both with the figures themselves and with their production. The line weathered the cancellation of the series, constant manufacturing delays, and a factory-destroying fire before Dapol lost the Doctor Who license in 2002. Their figures are badly painted, oddly articulated, and sometimes questionably accurate to the series. But like Kenner’s Star Wars line or Mego’s Star Trek , collectors look back fondly on the Dapol era, a time when there was thrill to just having a figure of a character like the Third Doctor or the Master. Today, the Dapol line may have been surpassed by Character Options’ still-running 5” Doctor Who line, but Dapol’s figures are still collected passionately by long-time Doctor Who fans, evidenced best by the nearly four-digit asking price for this 1987 TARDIS set .

Film and television tie-in toylines were largely avoided by manufacturers up until the 1970s . While this isn’t to say they didn’t happen, they usually consisted of low-cost, low-risk items, and not the kinds of elaborate action figure ranges we’ve come to expect. Doctor Who was no exception: while the series was immediately popular with children, British toy companies capitalized modestly. In the 1960s, Louis Marx manufactured several Dalek toys , but no accompanying Doctor or companions. The Marx Dalek was ubiquitous on U.K. shelves for years, and actually ended up in the series on two occasions. For the serials Evil of the Daleks and Planet of the Daleks , scores of the Louis Marx figures were put in the background of shots to make Dalek armies look larger. The Marx Dalek was the only figural Doctor Who toy produced for nearly fifteen years, with Denys Fisher providing the first-ever articulated action figure of the Doctor himself in 1978 . 

The Doctor was based on Tom Baker’s iconic incarnation of the Time Lord, complete with his signature scarf. He was accompanied by then-current companions Leela and robot dog K-9 , still fan-favorites fifty years on. The assortment of “villain” characters included the perennial Dalek, a Cyberman, and the K-1 Robot from Baker’s inaugural episode, the creatively titled “Robot.” Boxed or loose, the Denys Fisher figures and TARDIS are incredibly rare and collectible, with the Dalek and companion Leela valued at up to $1k mint in box. The Denys-Fisher TARDIS operated under the same principle as Mego’s Star Trek transporter playset, making figures “disappear” inside with the push of a button. Around the same time, Palitoy manufactured a talking Dalek and talking K-9. K-9 is the rarer of the two, and is a surprisingly detailed and screen-accurate item for its era. Despite arriving at the show’s arguable ratings peak (as well as its high-water mark creatively, if you ask many fans), neither the Palitoy nor the Denys-Fisher range were especially popular.

Dapol inherited the license at a ratings and creative nadir. Their line came to market in 1988, just in time for the series 25th Anniversary. In celebration, Dapol incorporated not only the series’ current Doctor (Sylvester McCoy), companion (Bonnie Langford’s Mel), and adversaries, but an assortment from across its history. By 1988, the series was running on fumes, having narrowly evaded cancellation in 1985. The first wave consisted of the 7th Doctor, Mel, K-9, the bat-like alien Tetrap, and four different Daleks. Dapol’s Daleks would be the longest-running and most expansive aspect of the line, with some two dozen Dalek variations produced in the fourteen years they held the Doctor Who license. The second wave arrived in 1989, just before the cancellation of the original series. It included the 4th Doctor (sans-scarf, a complaint of collectors for thirty-seven years and counting), companion Ace, a new Cyberman, and first-ever figures of Dalek creator Davros and the 2nd and 3rd Doctor foes the Ice Warriors. Bizarrely, the Ice Warrior came with an accessory reused from Hasbro’s G.I. Joe line. 

Two subsequent waves of new figures followed, bringing fans the 3rd Doctor (Jon Pertwee) and Roger Delgado’s incarnation of the Master, the “Melkur” statue from The Keeper of Traken , and four more aliens: a Time Lord, a Silurian, a Sea Devil, and a Sontaran. The alien sculpts are regarded as Dapol’s best work, detailed and fairly screen-accurate. Their human (and Time Lord) characters were criticized for soft likenesses and poor paint applications. Plastic quality and articulation were concerns across the line, the figures were brittle and prone to breakage. The line was rounded out by a TARDIS playset, at first just capturing the “police box” exterior of the vehicle, later resculpted to fold-out into the TARDIS’s interior, complete with plastic console.

While the fourth wave marked the end of the articulated line, a few unarticulated figures were produced in roughly the same scale as the articulated figures. These consisted of the 2nd Doctor (Patrick Troughton) and a Troughton-era Cyberman as seen in episodes The Moonbase and Tomb of the Cybermen . A planned “Whomobile” vehicle for the 3rd Doctor was cancelled following a devastating 1994 fire at their primary factory, this also ended production for most of the figures. Prototypes for a 1st Doctor figure and a Yeti (from the 2nd Doctor serial The Web of Fear ) were also cancelled; numerous rumored additional companions and aliens also failed to materialize.  Dapol continued to sell a limited number of characters (mostly surviving product from before the fire) and new Daleks up until 2002, when they lost the license. Character Options partnered with the BBC to take over the dormant license ahead of Doctor Who ’s 2005 return to screens, and still produce Doctor Who figures to this day. 

Character Options lived up to their name, releasing extensive product support for the 2005 season and the years after. For the first five seasons of the modern series, fans could expect that virtually every monster, alien, or adversary they saw on-screen would have an accompanying action figure; as well as a generous helping of companions, guest stars, and variants of the Doctor. In 2008, they expanded the range to include characters from the original series, and became the first-ever line to issue figures of every canon Doctor up to that point (the exception, of course, being Peter Cushing's Doctor from the 1960s theatrical films Dr. Who & The Daleks and Daleks Invasion Earth: 2150 A.D) . As Doctor Who ’s popularity has ebbed and flowed, the quantity of releases coming from Character Options has changed accordingly, but that same dedicated collector base that supported the Dapol line have kept the Character Options range running. This year, Character Options has finally issued the Yeti as a build-a-figure, making good on the promise of both Dapol’s prototype and their own long-delayed figure of the villain.

Who's your favorite Doctor? Leave a comment below and join the conversation now in the ComicBook Forum !

articles.title: This Intense 10/10 Stephen King Thriller Has Become a Free Streaming Obsession
articles.summary: Courtesy of Columbia Pictures There are many people out there who will claim to be Stephen King's number one fan, and if they are anything like one of his most terrifying creations then he would be nervous of ever leaving the house again. Yet, the trauma of one writer's encounter with an intense member of the public is the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There are many people out there who will claim to be Stephen King 's number one fan, and if they are anything like one of his most terrifying creations then he would be nervous of ever leaving the house again. Yet, the trauma of one writer's encounter with an intense member of the public is the premise of a Rob Reiner movie that became one of the best King adaptations of all time. Since arriving on free streaming platform Tubi, Misery has been attracting its own set of followers as the movie has found its way into the Top 10 on the streamer. As one of the most intense and unforgettable psychological thrillers ever made, Misery may not get you in the mood for the festive holidays, but it will make you think twice about those dreams of becoming famous.

The story of Misery is a simple one. Author Paul Sheldon (James Caan) is injured in a bad car crash but that is the least of his worries when he is "rescued" by Annie Wilkes (the impeccably unhinged Kathy Bates), a woman who claims to be his number one fan. While this suggests that he is in good hands, Sheldon soon discovers that his savior could actually be the death of him when she discovers that he has killed off her favorite character in his latest novel and decides that he needs to rethink his decision and bring them back from the dead. As the story unfolds, it becomes a tale of survival for Sheldon as he attempts to work out how to escape his biggest fan. The battle of wits is one that mostly plays out in a two-hander, single-room scenario, but proves that some movies don't need huge special effects budgets and a cast of thousands to enthral and audience.

For most of the 1980s, the mere mention of Stephen King's involvement in a movie meant hokey supernatural tales of monsters, ghosts, aliens, and plenty of films that were almost as laughable as they were scary. In 1990, though, Reiner's Misery proved that King's work was never really about the creatures and spooky elements, it was about how the humans in his stories reacted and coped through the horrors. In making the "monster" of Misery a woman who you could have passed on the street, audiences are given a very strong message that it isn't just the things under the bed or in the closet that can do horrifying things while smiling. For her chilling portrayal of Annie Wilkes, Kathy Bates earned herself an Oscar, among many other awards, even if the film failed to pick up any other Academy Awards despite definitely deserving them.

When it comes to naming the greatest Stephen King adaptations ever, there have been some strong contenders in recent years with the likes of The Long Walk, The Life of Chuck , and Doctor Sleep , but it is hard to match the run of 1990s releases that began with Misery , included The Shawshank Redemption, and ended with The Green Mile . One thing for certain is that there is always an abundance of new King adaptations being developed, with some upcoming projects including movie versions of recent novels like Fairy Tale and Billy Summers , as well as older ones like the remake of The Mist and the long awaited Dark Tower project that could be on track to finally happen at Amazon MGM Studios under the guidance of Mike Flanagan. Regardless of what new movies and TV are made, though, there is something about King classics like Misery that make them timeless tales of terror that will be enjoyed by audiences for years to come. You can watch Misery for free now on Tubi.

What is your favorite Stephen King adaptation? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: Marvel Is Bringing Back One of the X-Men's Most Dangerous Villains to Face Its Most Dysfunctional Team
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Marvel Comics There is a new Marvel mutant title that has teamed up one of the most dysfunctional teams in X-Men comics history. As is always the case in Marvel, there are several mutant titles on the market right now, with different X-Men teams situated around the country, one as far away as Alaska and another down […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There is a new Marvel mutant title that has teamed up one of the most dysfunctional teams in X-Men comics history. As is always the case in Marvel, there are several mutant titles on the market right now, with different X-Men teams situated around the country, one as far away as Alaska and another down in New Orleans. Add in the Wolverine titles and even one with X-23 and her clones, and there is a lot going on for the mutants right now in the Marvel Universe. Now, the most dysfunctional team has formed to defeat a greater evil. This team formed in a comic book called X-Orcists .

X-Orcists #1 (2026) by Ashley Allen and German Peralta sees a team that includes Magik, Madelyne Pryor, and Juggernaut teaming up to battle one of the X-Men's most dangerous villains. Seeing a redeemed former villain, one of the X-Men's most violent members, and an antihero who tried to destroy the world once teaming up seems strange, but considering the villain, it is very important.

X-Orcists #1 opens with a scene from West Texas where an annual carnival was in action, but it was all ruined when something possessed a mutant who was part of a sideshow involving fire. Whatever possessed him turned him into a giant creature, and he began to slaughter the people watching his show. What happened next was that Madelyne Pryor woke up in the middle of the devastation, and when she stood up and looked around, she realized she needed to figure out what had happened. Soon, something tried to get into her mind, and she fought it off. This was important, as one panel showed a vision of Mister Sinister, with Madelyne vowing that no one would control her again.

As always, when it comes to unexpected team-ups, the teammates had to start off by fighting each other. Magik and Juggernaut showed up when Cerebro detected mutant activity, and they saw all the dead bodies with Madelyne Pryor standing among them. Without asking what happened, Magik and Juggernaut attacked Madelyne, even as the former villain tried to explain that she didn't do this. Neither Juggernaut nor Magik would listen to her until the possessed fire mutant attacked them.

It was an old trope from comics, movies, and TV shows, where the reluctant teammates fight each other before being forced to team up to fight the real villains. By the time the demon attacked, Juggernaut realized it was trying to get into his head, the same as it had with Madelyne earlier. It also tried to get into Magik's head, but she fought it off as well. This was when Magik realized the threat was coming from Limbo , and that it couldn't have been a Limbo demon possessing another demon. The demon was possessing mutants and humans.

After a demonic dog-looking creature burst out of the mutant's chest, killing him instantly, it looked for another person to possess and chose a young man who was hiding after the initial attack. After that, it jumped to that man's girlfriend, who was trying to help him, but she died when the demon escaped her body. Magik realized they needed to figure out what this threat was, which meant working with Madelyne Pryor. What was scary was that neither Madelyne Pryor nor Magik could identify the demon, and its powers neutralized Pryor's psychic powers.

Magik admitted that Madelyne was losing control, despite being the woman who was supposed to be ruling over Limbo. Magik also realized that this being a demon she knew nothing about meant it was hidden from even Belasco , making it a possible fail-safe that she was not equipped to deal with alone. The creature was from the depths of Limbo, and Madelyne admitted that she had felt something trying to get into her head, and she had to fight it off. By the end of the issue, we learn who is responsible, although the three dysfunctional mutants don't know yet.

Selene is back. This was shown in a scene that took place in Chester, Massachusetts, where what looked like a cult was summoning something. This ended with them bringing forth Selene, and she held two items that tie into both Limbo heavyweights. In one hand, Selene held Magik's Soulsword, which was constructed of the life force of Illyana Rasputin and was forged in Limbo. As for the weapon in her other hand, it was the Scythe of Sorrows, a unique weapon that Madelyne was able to manifest, similar to Magik's Soulsword, but one that channeled her emotional pain and regret into a weapon. This was after Magik transferred leadership of Limbo to Madelyne. How Selene got these weapons remains a mystery, but it would also explain why she has the advantage in this new battle.

What are your thoughts on the new X-Orcists comic book series? Let us know where you think this series is headed in the comments below.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Ever since superhero comics started, the industry has created its fair share of femmes fatales like Catwoman , the deadly women who are based on the classic noir character types. A femme fatale in detective stories and film noir is a deadly or fatal woman who often uses seduction and her charms to lead lovers into compromising or deadly traps. These are women who know they have complete control over any man who crosses their path, and they use this to their advantage in every situation. This became a perfect character trait to add to several deadly antiheroes and villains in comics over the years, including one of its most popular characters whose name identifies her as a classic femme fatale, and another who is one of DC's most popular antiheroes.

This trope has been around since the start of comics. Catwoman debuted as the Cat in Batman #1 (1940), and Will Eisner's The Spirit was full of femmes fatales like P'Gell and Sand Saref. In fact, Sand Saref was the direct inspiration for Elektra, whom Frank Miller created years later. The appeal of these characters is simple, as they attack a hero's heart and judgment instead of his body, and most can't fight that.

Black Widow made her debut in Tales of Suspense #52 (1964) by Stan Lee, Don Rico, and Don Heck. Her name completely ties into her role as a femme fatale, as a "black widow" is defined as a woman who murders one or more husbands or romantic partners. At the start, Natasha Romanova was a non-costumed Soviet spy sent with partner Boris to infiltrate Stark Industries and kill Russian defector Anton Vanko. Stark was her original target, but she soon became the love interest of Hawkeye.

Hawkeye and Black Widow both ended up becoming heroes, and she joined the Avengers in Avengers #111 (1973) after working with them as an ally for a few years. She slipped up sometimes, including when she was brainwashed and brought in the Swordsman and Power Man to attack the Avengers in Avengers #29 (1966). She also became Daedevil's love interest for a time.

Madame Masque debuted as Big M , a Maggia boss, in Tales of Suspense #97 (1967). Her name was revealed to be Whitney Frost in issue #98, and she became Madame Masque in Iron Man #17 (1969). She was born as Giulietta Nefaria, daughter of the criminal Count Nefaria, and raised as Whitney Frost. She took over her father's Maggia family after he was jailed. Her face was scarred in a plane crash after a failed raid on Stark Industries, and the criminal Mordecai Midas gave her the golden mask. The crash explains her hatred of Tony Stark.

She got close to Tony Stark by posing as his secretary, Krissy Longfellow, and the two became lovers. Eventually, Tony learned who she was, and she learned he was Iron Man. The affair ended in Iron Man #116 when Count Nefaria was nearly killed fighting Iron Man, and Whitney sided with her father. She has no superpowers, and one of her most powerful weapons is her charm and ability to manipulate the men around her.

Poison Ivy made her debut in Batman #181 (1966) by Robert Kanigher and Sheldon Moldoff. From her introduction, she was created to be a femme fatale. In her first appearance, she was attracted to Batman and brewed love potions to ensnare him. She eventually became a more complex character in the 1980s when her origin was rewritten in Secret Origins #36 (1988) to make her Dr. Pamela Isley, a botanist, who was injected with poisons and toxins by her mentor Jason Woodrue (the Floronic Man).

In the same story of her new origin, "Pavane," she said she moved to Gotham City to get Batman's attention. In "Hothouse" (from Batman: Legends of the Dark Knight #42-43 (1993)), she kissed Batman and tried to unmask him. In "Hush," she used pheromones to hypnotize Superman, putting DC's strongest hero under her control. This carried over to the movies, where she also used pheromones in Batman & Robin .

Felicia Hardy debuted in The Amazing Spider-Man #194 (1979) by Marv Wolfman and Dave Cockrum, and became Marvel's version of the Black Cat. While Catwoman became a femme fatale for Batman, Black Cat was the same for Spider-Man . She is the daughter of cat burglar Walter Hardy, whom she broke out of custody so he could die at home, despite Spider-Man trying to stop her. Since her introduction, her relationship with Spider-Man has defined her career, as she tries to do better for him.

In Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #87 (1983) by Bill Mantlo and Al Milgrom, Peter took his mask off for her, and she begged him to put it back on to keep the mystery. Black Cat accepted bad-luck superpowers from a secret benefactor who turned out to be the Kingpin. Spider-Man ended the relationship when the powers endangered him, and she refused to reveal their source. She has since become more of a hero than a villain, although she still has her moments of misdeeds.

The most famous femme fatale in comic book history was also its first. Catwoman debuted in Batman #1 (1940) by Bill Finger and Bob Kane. At the time, she was known as the Cat, a jewel thief who disguised herself as an older woman. The big thing to note about this was that Batman seemed to deliberately allow her to escape rather than bring her in. Catwoman was based on classic femme fatale movie actresses like Jean Harlow and Hedy Lamarr.

She became very popular thanks to the Batman television series from the 1960s, where she was played by three different actresses. In "Hush," she and Batman became lovers, and he revealed his identity, but he ended it after suspecting Hush and the Riddler had manipulated them. She and Batman almost got married as well, but she was the one who broke off the wedding, saying it would kill the drive that made him Batman.

Who is your favorite femme fatale in comics? Let us know your favorites in the comments below.

articles.title: The Most Underrated Star Trek: Deep Space Nine Episode Is Also One of Its Best
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Skydance Star Trek: Deep Space Nine has a certain reputation with Star Trek fans. The third Star Trek show, it debuted in 1993 and ran until 1999. It was the first Trek show to experiment with serialized storytelling, while incorporating the standard monster of the week episodes (in Trek parlance, they're sometimes called "anomalies of the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Star Trek: Deep Space Nine has a certain reputation with Star Trek fans. The third Star Trek show, it debuted in 1993 and ran until 1999. It was the first Trek show to experiment with serialized storytelling, while incorporating the standard monster of the week episodes (in Trek parlance, they're sometimes called "anomalies of the week") that were just as much about building the characters up for the lore episodes that would be the anchor of each season. Deep Space Nine has become a favorite of Trek fans for numerous reasons, but the biggest was that it was different than any other Trek we'd gotten. The connections it built between the cast and the audience made everything hit that much harder, allowing the show's episodes to reach some amazing heights, even if not all of them get the recognition they deserve.

Every era of Star Trek has amazing episodes , but Deep Space Nine has a surplus of them. Episodes like "Duet", "The Visitor", "Far Beyond the Stars", "In the Pale Moonlight", and "Under the Paper Moon" get the lion's share of the praise, but there's one episode that deserves way more praise than it gets. The seventh season of the show has its ups and downs (the last seven episode stretch is one of my favorite finale build-ups ever, but there are too many Ezri episodes earlier episodes earlier in the season), but there's one episode that blew me away when I first saw it – "The Siege of AR-558". This episode is one of the most harrowing episodes in Trek history and an underrated gem.

Star Trek: Deep Space Nine was different from other Trek in a variety of ways. To begin with, it was set on a space station and not a starship. Captain Sisko was the first black Captain and the show played heavily with religious themes related to him and the Bajoran people. The show was more character-focused than science-focused, and it told different kind of stories. It also went in a direction that previous Trek really only toyed with – the Federation at war.

The inciting incident of the show was the discovery of the Bajoran wormhole leading to the Gamma Quadrant and in the second season we were introduced to the Dominion, a mysterious power from the far side of the galaxy. Season Three would reveal that the Founders were the Changelings, Security Chief Odo's race, who ruled the Dominion, leading to a cold war throughout the season. The fourth season would see a war between the Cardassians and the Klingons covertly started by the Dominion, with Starfleet eventually fighting the Klingons, before the truth was revealed. The Cardassians joined the Dominion, and the Klingons and Federation teamed back up.

Seasons Four, Five, Six, and Seven gave us something that we'd never seen in Trek history. Sure, we had seen ship to ship battles for years, and the Original Series revolved around the ongoing conflict between the Federation and the Klingons, but we'd never seen a shooting war. Deep Space Nine gave us that and it was awesome. However, most of the show's battles were still ship to ship. We barely got to see the actual ground war against the Dominion and their genetically engineered soldiers the Jem'Hadar until the eighth episode of Season Seven, "The Siege of AR-558".

The episode saw the U.S.S. Defiant bring supplies to a Starfleet outpost on AR-558 in the Chin'Toka System. The position had been under siege for months with no relief troops sent in. They were surrounded by cloaked Houdini mines – invisible explosives that would chase you down – and constantly under attack. Jem'Hadar ships end up attacking the Defiant , with Sisko ordering the ship away and volunteering to take command of AR-558 until it can return.

For years, we were used to Starfleet as the smiling good guys, always bringing succor and aid to anyone who needed it. They were clean and civilized, their ships basically flying luxury hotels in the stars, especially by the time we got to the 24th century of the TNG/DS9/VOY era of the show. We saw them struggle at times, but we had never seen like this. I think the best way to describe this episode is that it's a Vietnam movie.

The Starfleet officers are like the naive young recruits from 'Nam movies at the halfway point. They had experienced horrors the likes of which they never imagined and it changed them. One of the officers, Reese, had begun to take the ketracel white tubes – the addictive drug that kept the Jem'Hadar under the Founders' control – which is a direct reference to every crazy soldier who collected body parts of the people they killed in Vietnam movie. We get to spend time with these stressed out, injured, mentally beaten men and women, seeing what happened when Starfleet met a situation they couldn't just technobabble their way through.

That said, technobabble does end up helping to save the day, when Sisko and company are able to suborn the Houdinis and turn them against the Jem'Hadar, but this isn't your typical "monster of the week" episode. It technically fits into the overarching arc of the season, but it is a standalone episode as far as the story it starts ends in the same episode. The episode, though, does have repercussions for the main cast, in the form of Nog. Or, in this case, Nog's leg.

The Ferengi Nog's arc from vaguely criminal kid to Starfleet officer is one the best in the show. His uncle Quark was completely against his nephew joining Starfleet, believing it not a place for a Ferengi. However, Nog was always able to come through without a scratch, something that would end in this episode. His hearing made him an amazing scout and while on patrol, he was shot in the leg. Jem'Hadar weapons were designed to be especially damaging and his leg had to be removed. It's a harrowing moment, watching this young character who had grown so much so gravely injured.

The episode's final battle scene is the heartbreaking center of the story. We had grown attached to these soldiers throughout the episode and the final charge of the Jem'Hadar would be the end of several of them (Reese survives; sci-fi legend Bill Mumy's character Kellin doesn't). Star Trek actions scenes always seem so safe; sure we see red shirts die all the time, but there's never really a sense of danger. Deep Space Nine had several ground combat scenes and they were always able to impart that sense of death around the corner that the best battle scenes could. "The Siege of AR-558″'s final scene is everything you could want from that perspective. The ending, with the soldiers being relieved as a new group takes over the outpost, is the perfect denouement for this episode, leaving viewers with the sense of more meat being loaded into the meat grinder.

Deep Space Nine was always a cut above the others . It was unique back then in the pantheon of both Trek and sci-fi TV in general, and no other Trek series has ever reached the same level. The show combined many of the best writers from TNG and was able to show that Star Trek didn't have to just be science-based monster of the week; it could tell a long coherent story over the course of the entire series. I just did a rewatch last year and it's one of the few Trek series that is basically great the entire time; even TNG was bad for most of the first two seasons (seriously, don't watch Season One at all after "Encounter at Farpoint"; there's not much good there).

The show is able to stand up so well because of how well it built its characters and the unique stories that you could only do with Deep Space Nine . "The Siege of AR-558" took the idea of the Federation at war to its ultimate extent – what happens when the scientists and ambassadors and engineers have to get down in the filth with the foot soldiers. I missed the first run of the last season of DS9 . I was 18 and had others things to do at 7:00pm on a Sunday in 1998 and 1999. I caught a rerun of it a few months after the show ended and was blown away. It was completely different from any other Trek I had ever watched and it stuck with me in a way few others episodes have. Nog's screams are unforgettable, the death knell of the innocence of Starfleet. War is hell, even when you have replicators and holosuites back home.

What do you think about "The Siege of AR-558"? Do you think it stands up or did it fail to deliver on its premise? Sound off in the comment section below.
